results.title: MRI-guided thrombolysis for stroke with unknown time of onset (WAKE-UP)

results.authors: Ma H, Campbell BCV, Parsons MW, et al.
results.key_finding: In patients 4.5 to 9 hours from onset, or with wake-up stroke within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep, who had salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging (core under 70 mL, mismatch ratio above 1.2, mismatch volume above 10 mL) and no planned thrombectomy, IV alteplase increased excellent functional outcome at 90 days, with more symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage.
results.title: Thrombolysis guided by perfusion imaging up to 9 hours after onset of stroke (EXTEND)

results.authors: Prabhakaran S, Gonzalez NR, Zachrison KS, et al.
results.key_finding: For wake-up or unknown-onset stroke, IV thrombolysis is reasonable either with a DWI-positive, FLAIR-negative lesion, or within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep with salvageable penumbra on automated perfusion imaging in patients not eligible for thrombectomy.
results.title: 2026 AHA/ASA guideline for the early management of patients with acute ischemic stroke

output.summary: Two imaging pathways select wake-up or unknown-onset stroke patients for IV thrombolysis: a DWI-FLAIR mismatch (WAKE-UP), and, within 9 hours of the midpoint of sleep in patients not eligible for thrombectomy, penumbral mismatch on automated perfusion imaging (EXTEND criteria: core under 70 mL, ratio above 1.2, mismatch above 10 mL). A FLAIR-positive lesion closes only the first pathway.

Refer for left carotid endarterectomy (or stenting if surgical risk is high) between 2 days and 2 weeks after the stroke: a symptomatic moderate (about 65%) ipsilateral stenosis with irregular plaque in a 67-year-old man with a prior event in the same territory favors revascularization when perioperative risk is below 6% (AHA/ASA 2021 secondary prevention), and the paroxysmal AF does not remove this indication. His wife reports that he went to bed at approximately 22:30 last night and was entirely at his baseline, having watched the evening news and conversed normally before falling asleep. She awoke at 06:15 this morning and found him already sitting on the edge of the bed. He told her he felt 'off' and she immediately noticed his speech was slurred. When he tried to stand, he stumbled slightly to the right side and had difficulty buttoning his shirt with his right hand. She drove him to the emergency department, arriving at 07:40. The patient himself reports that he woke up around 06:00 and noticed his right hand felt 'clumsy' and his mouth felt 'thick.' He denies any headache, visual changes, nausea, or vomiting. He did not experience any chest pain, palpitations, or shortness of breath. There was no witnessed seizure activity. He denies any recent fever, neck stiffness, or trauma. He admits he has not been taking his blood pressure medications consistently over the past week because he ran out and had not yet refilled the prescriptions. He also acknowledges continued smoking despite medical advice. His wife notes that he has been snoring more heavily than usual over the past several months and has not been using his CPAP device for over a year. She recalls his prior TIA episode two years ago presented similarly with transient right hand clumsiness that resolved within an hour, but this time the symptoms have persisted. Last known well time is established as 22:30 the prior evening, approximately 9 hours before ED arrival.
